title: How to keep your house cool
text: This story is featured in the June 17, 2026 edition of Healthy Living. Visit our Special Sections page to read the whole magazine.This summer is set to be hotter than normal. And in the Southeast, it will also be drier.That sweltering weather will have you trying anything to stay cool. If you don't want to break the bank turning the air conditioning up, check out these methods instead. Use fans, shades Tried and true, shades are an easy way to keep the sun and heat out of your home. Covering windows that face south and west minimizes direct light in the afternoon, which will keep indoor temperatures lower. You can also add reflective film for a unique twist. The film is meant to let light in while also redirecting heat and ultraviolet light rays. Metalized or carbon films are the most effective at reducing heat. Additionally, electric fans are efficient to help cool the air in your home. While fans by themselves just move air around, putting a bowl of ice in front of one can simulate a spraying mist. Fans should also be positioned strategically, especially during extreme heat. Putting a fan in a closed room in hot temperatures does nothing to relieve the heat. Fans are most effective when placed to draw in cooler air or expel hot air from interior rooms. Putting one at the bottom of a set of stairs, tilted upward, also helps circulate air from floor to floor. Ceiling fans should rotate counterclockwise in the summer to create a downdraft. Covering windows that face south and west minimizes direct light in the afternoon, which will keep indoor temperatures lower. Photo by Darren Richardson on Unsplash. DARREN RICHARDSON/UNSPLASH Check the weather, doors and windows There's nothing better than a cool breeze in the summer — but you should be mindful of when you're letting the outside in. Close the windows if the outside temperature is hotter than your home, and open them when the outdoors are cooler. You should also check your doors and windows for gaps and drafts. More than a quarter of your home's cooling energy loss can be lost through cracks. Weather stripping can help close any existing cracks along your entrances. To find gaps in a window, try holding a candle or match next to the frame and look for fluttering. To look for cracks under closed doors, try pulling a piece of paper out from under it. If it's easy to pull out, it probably needs a new weather strip. Closing doors and vents of unused rooms also helps concentrate your cooling efforts to your main rooms. Other creative alternatives Turning off kitchen and laundry appliances that generate heat can keep your house cool. Consider grilling outside on hot days, or hanging your clothes out to dry. A switch to LED light bulbs — rather than heat-producing incandescent or halogen options — will also help maintain cool. Finally, investing in other home updates can provide a long-term solution for heat. Trees and scrubs can reduce heat, along with porous or rock driveways in place of cement or blacktops. Solar panels can provide shade and reduce your home's reliance on fossil fuels. And upgraded insulation doesn't just help your home stay warm in the winter; it also keeps heat out during the summer. Air conditioning If you do use your air conditioning, make sure the unit is cleaned and serviced with new filters, especially if you have a central or window unit. This will make sure your system is working at maximum efficiency. The American Lung Association also recommends "swamp coolers," or evaporative air conditioning units. These devices can cool the air by 5 to 15 degrees by evaporating water, which absorbs heat in the process. They also require less maintenance and cost than traditional units, although they are not as effective. The ALA recommends them for dry climates and notes that users should open doors during use to increase air flow. The units should also be cleaned up to four times a year.
